title: Tree Row by Row
statement:
You get the root of a binary tree. Return its values grouped by level: a list of rows, where row 0 holds the root, row 1 holds the root's children, and so on.

Inside each row, list values from left to right, even when neighbours in a row have different parents. An empty tree gives an empty list.

Trees are written in level order with null for a missing child.

examples.why: 2 is a child of 6 while 13 and 19 are children of 15; they still share a row. A plain breadth-first walk would give the right order but lose the row breaks: [11, 6, 15, 2, 13, 19, 4].
One row with one value. It is still a list inside a list.

constraints: The tree is at most 500 levels deep
hints: Which data structure hands nodes back in the order you discovered them?
A queue visits nodes in level order already. The missing piece is knowing where one level ends and the next begins.
At the start of each round, the queue holds exactly one full level. Read its length, take out exactly that many nodes into a new row, and push their children for the next round.

explain.intuition:
Breadth-first search with a queue visits nodes in exactly the order this problem wants: the root, then everything one step away, then everything two steps away, each level from left to right. The only thing BFS does not give you for free is the row breaks.

The trick is to notice what the queue holds at the start of each round: exactly one complete level, and nothing else. So read its size first, then take out that many nodes. Their children go to the back of the queue and form the next level. Those nodes are the row. The alternative is depth-first search carrying a depth number: each node appends its value to rows[depth]. Because DFS visits left before right, each row still fills left to right. BFS matches how the problem is phrased; DFS is handy when you are already doing a recursive walk for something else.
steps: If the root is null, return [].
Put the root in a queue.
While the queue is not empty: let size be its current length and start an empty row.
Repeat size times: take a node out, add its value to row, and push its left then right child if they exist.
Add row to the result, and return the result when the queue is empty.
pitfalls: Using the queue length as the loop bound while pushing children into the same queue. The bound grows during the loop and levels run together. Save the size first.
Pushing the right child before the left one. Each row comes out reversed.
Returning [[]] for an empty tree instead of [].

complexity.space: O(w) for BFS (w = widest level), O(h) extra for DFS

solutions.title: BFS, one level per round
solutions.idea: At the start of each round the queue holds one whole level. Take out exactly that many nodes as a row and queue their children.

solutions.title: DFS with a depth index
solutions.idea: Walk the tree depth-first, left before right, carrying the depth. Append each value to rows[depth], creating the row the first time that depth is reached.

followups: Return the rows in zigzag order: left to right, then right to left, alternating.
Return the rows from the bottom level up. Can you do it without reversing at the end?
